stories.headline: Federal Judge Strikes Down Trump Administration's $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee as Unlawful Tax
stories.summary:
A federal judge in Boston on Monday invalidated the Trump administration's $100,000 annual fee on H-1B visa applications, ruling it an unlawful tax that violated both federal administrative law and the Constitution. U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin sided with a coalition of 20 Democratic-led state attorneys general who argued the administration exceeded its authority and usurped Congress's power to set immigration policy and taxation.

Trump announced the fee via executive order last year, dramatically raising the cost of obtaining the visa used primarily by highly skilled foreign workers in technology, engineering, and other fields. Critics argued the fee was effectively a tax that could only be imposed by Congress, not the executive branch. Supporters of the fee contended it was a legitimate tool to protect American workers and manage immigration flows.

The ruling is a significant legal setback for the administration's efforts to curtail high-skilled immigration through executive action. The H-1B program is heavily utilized by major U.S. technology companies to hire workers from India, China, and elsewhere. The administration is expected to appeal the decision.

stories.headline: Apple Expected to Unveil Revised AI Strategy at WWDC as New CEO Faces Siri Pressure
stories.summary:
Apple is expected Monday to detail its artificial intelligence roadmap at its annual Worldwide Developers Conference, marking the second consecutive year the company has used the event primarily to lay out its AI ambitions. Unlike competitors such as Google and Microsoft, Apple has not reorganized its corporate structure around AI, a distinction the company is expected to address.

The conference serves as an early major test for incoming CEO John Ternus, who took over the company's top role this year. Central to his immediate challenges is a long-delayed overhaul of the Siri voice assistant, which has fallen significantly behind rival AI-powered assistants in capability and public perception. Analysts and investors are watching the announcement closely for signs of whether Apple can close the gap.

Apple has faced persistent criticism that its AI features, marketed under the Apple Intelligence brand, have been slow to roll out and incremental compared to offerings from Google, Amazon, and OpenAI. The WWDC keynote is expected to provide a clearer timeline and scope for upcoming releases across iPhone, iPad, and Mac platforms.

stories.headline: 'Schmigadoon!' Wins Best Musical, 'Liberation' Takes Best Play at 79th Tony Awards
stories.summary:
"Schmigadoon!", an adaptation of the Apple TV+ series that parodies golden-age Broadway musicals, won the Tony Award for Best New Musical on Sunday at the 79th annual ceremony in New York. Creator Cinco Paul won Tonys for both the score and the book, completing a redemption arc after the original series was canceled after two seasons. Apple became the first studio to achieve an unofficial "studio EGOT" — winning major awards across all four top ceremonies — through the win.

Bess Wohl's "Liberation," a drama about a consciousness-raising women's group in 1970s Ohio, won Best New Play, making Wohl only the fourth woman to win the prize. The play had also won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama earlier this year, joining a short list of 18 works to achieve both honors. "Death of a Salesman" led all productions with six Tonys, including Best Play Revival, with Laurie Metcalf winning her third Tony for her performance alongside Nathan Lane.

"Ragtime" won Best Musical Revival, and Caissie Levy won Best Actress in a Musical for her role in the production. The ceremony recognized a Broadway season marked by strong revivals alongside new works, with the revival category drawing some of the evening's most notable performances and design awards.

stories.headline: Peru Election Too Close to Call as Vote Count Continues
stories.summary:
Peru's presidential election is deadlocked, with early tallies from pollster Ipsos showing left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez at 50.3% and right-wing veteran Keiko Fujimori at 49.7%. With more than 91% of official votes counted, the race remains statistically tied and a recount is widely expected, a process that could drag on for weeks as it did in 2021.

Sánchez, a former minister under jailed ex-president Pedro Castillo, is counting on rural Andean ballots still being tallied to extend his narrow lead. Fujimori, running for the presidency for the fourth time, is insisting that every ballot sheet be counted before any winner is declared, calling it 'irresponsible' to project a result from early samples. Sánchez has pledged to seek a presidential pardon for Castillo if elected.

The election pits sharply divergent visions for Peru against each other. Fujimori has campaigned on a military-style crackdown on organized crime and extortion, leaning into the legacy of her father, former president Alberto Fujimori, who was jailed for crimes against humanity but is credited by supporters with defeating violent insurgencies. Sánchez is promising broad economic reforms.

Peru has now held ten presidential elections in roughly a decade, reflecting deep political instability. The 2021 race between the same two candidates took weeks to resolve, and analysts expect a similar prolonged process this time.

stories.headline: House Oversight Report Alleges Walz Administration Ignored Billions in Social Services Fraud
stories.summary:
A Republican-led House Oversight Committee released a 205-page final report Monday alleging that senior Minnesota officials, including then-Gov. Tim Walz, failed for years to act on repeated internal warnings about fraud in the state's federal nutrition and Medicaid programs. The report estimates Minnesota lost at least $300 million in stolen federal nutrition funds meant to feed children during COVID-19, and that as much as $9 billion in Medicaid billing may have been fraudulent — an estimate attributed to a federal prosecutor but disputed by Walz administration officials.

Congressional investigators spoke to nearly 30 whistleblowers, some of whom accused the Walz administration of retaliating against state employees who raised fraud concerns. The report alleges that fears of racial discrimination claims — rather than legal constraints — contributed to the administration's decision to continue payments to providers suspected of fraud. More than 110 individuals have been federally charged in connection with various Minnesota fraud schemes, many linked to the now-defunct Feeding Our Future nonprofit.

The committee found that Walz was allegedly aware of fraud associated with Feeding Our Future as early as 2020, but payments continued for roughly two more years, and that Walz gave conflicting accounts of when he first learned of the scheme. House Oversight Chairman James Comer has asked Vice President JD Vance to scrutinize fraud-prevention deficiencies in Minnesota's social services programs in the wake of the report's release.

Walz administration officials have disputed the most sweeping fraud estimates. The findings carry heightened political significance given Walz's role as the 2024 Democratic vice-presidential nominee, and Democrats have not yet issued a formal response to Monday's report.

stories.headline: Update: Pope Leo XIV Demands Reparations for Clergy Abuse Survivors in Address to Spanish Bishops
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV used his visit to Spain on Monday to issue a direct demand to the country's Catholic hierarchy to provide reparations to survivors of clergy sexual abuse, calling on the church to offer 'listening, truth, justice, and reparation' to victims. The address came ahead of an expected meeting with abuse survivors during his weeklong stay and represented one of the most assertive statements by a sitting pope on the Spanish church's decades-long failure to confront the crisis.

Spain launched a reparations system earlier this year for clerical abuse cases too old to be prosecuted, an unusual arrangement that gives the Spanish government a strong role in the process and the final say in payouts. The system is not legally binding, and advocacy groups have offered mixed assessments — praising its structure while expressing skepticism about implementation.

Several survivor groups said they were left uninformed about the details of their planned meeting with the pope and held a small protest outside the Vatican's embassy in Madrid. A spokesperson for the Robbed Childhood association said the selected survivors were 'being used by the church to clean up the image of a Spanish church that has never been able to live up to its victims.'

Leo also reaffirmed the Catholic Church's position on the confidentiality of confession, pushing back against efforts in several European countries to legally require priests to report abuse disclosures made during the sacrament. Independent investigations have previously identified confession secrecy as a barrier to accountability in abuse cases.

stories.headline: World Cup Fans Blocked by U.S. Travel Bans and Visa Suspensions Ahead of Matches
stories.summary:
Supporters from more than a quarter of the nations competing in the 2026 FIFA World Cup face U.S. travel bans, tighter visa restrictions, or high rejection rates, according to BBC World Service analysis of travel data. Fans from Haiti, Iran, Senegal, and Ivory Coast — all World Cup participants — are barred from receiving the standard visitor visa recommended for attending matches, a direct result of President Trump's travel ban list.

The disruptions extend beyond the formal ban list. After the outbreak of U.S.-involved hostilities with Iran, the U.S. suspended routine consular services in Iraq, leaving Iraqi fans with no in-country visa option despite Iraq not being on the travel ban. One Iraqi fan told the BBC he spent $1,800 traveling to Jordan for a visa appointment, only to be turned away because he was not a Jordanian citizen.

Fan associations from affected countries have reacted with anger. A spokesperson for Ivory Coast's national supporters' group called the restrictions 'a form of segregation that doesn't dare speak its name,' noting that no European nation faces comparable barriers. The group decided not to attempt sending fans to the U.S. at all.

U.S. authorities have defended their visa system as necessary to manage border security and the large volume of people entering the country. The controversy adds a significant diplomatic and reputational dimension to the United States' role as host of the world's most-watched sporting event.

stories.headline: Update: Houthis Declare Complete Ban on Israeli Ships in Red Sea
stories.summary:
Yemen's Houthi movement, an Iran-backed militant group controlling much of the country, announced a total ban on Israeli-flagged vessels transiting the Red Sea. The declaration adds a new dimension to the regional conflict, threatening a maritime corridor that has served as a critical bypass route for shipping that might otherwise use the Strait of Hormuz.

The move comes as tensions between Iran and Israel are escalating sharply, with fresh missile exchanges reported Monday. The Houthis previously conducted sustained drone and missile campaigns against Red Sea shipping during earlier phases of the Israel-Gaza conflict, disrupting global trade and forcing shipping companies to reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope at significant additional cost.

A renewed Houthi blockade of Israeli shipping in the Red Sea would compound pressure on global supply chains already strained by the broader Iran-Israel conflict. The combination of a potential Strait of Hormuz disruption and Red Sea restrictions could significantly affect energy and goods transportation worldwide.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Abruptly Ends 'Meet the Press' Interview After Clashing With Host Over Election Claims and Anti-Weaponization Fund
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump cut short a live interview with NBC's 'Meet the Press' host Kristen Welker on Sunday, walking out after a series of confrontational exchanges over his claims of election fraud, California ballot counting, and his proposed $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. Trump told Welker, 'You're a one-sided crooked network. Sorry. Let's call it quits because I've had enough,' before ending the interview.

The sharpest exchanges came over the anti-weaponization fund, which Trump has promoted as compensation for people he says were targeted by the Biden administration. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche previously stated the administration would not move forward with the fund, but Trump told Welker he still personally supported the idea and believed it would need congressional approval to proceed. Trump also repeated unsubstantiated claims that the 2020 election was rigged.

Supporters of Trump praised his willingness to confront what they characterize as a hostile press, while critics and media observers argued that a sitting president walking out of a major Sunday news program interview was itself a significant and unprecedented moment. The exchange also brought renewed attention to internal Republican tensions over the weaponization fund proposal, which had drawn opposition from members of his own party before being shelved.

stories.headline: South Africa Xenophobia Crisis: Malawians Repatriated as Multiple Nations Evacuate Citizens
stories.summary:
A group of 150 Malawians departed South Africa on Monday amid growing fears of xenophobic violence, with authorities in Lilongwe organizing ground transport for nationals who had taken refuge in temporary camps in Mossel Bay, Western Cape. The repatriation follows reports of door-to-door intimidation targeting foreign nationals and the deaths of two Mozambicans in the area. Ghana, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe have also organized repatriation flights and ground transport for their own citizens in recent days.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa addressed the nation Sunday, announcing new measures to accelerate the deportation of undocumented migrants while warning South Africans against taking the law into their own hands. 'There is no space for xenophobia, racism, sexism, Afrophobia or any other forms of intolerance,' Ramaphosa said. Anti-migrant groups have set a June 30 deadline demanding undocumented migrants leave the country.

The crisis has triggered a diplomatic dispute between South Africa and Ghana, with South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola accusing his Ghanaian counterpart of spreading misinformation about the scale and nature of the violence. Ghana's foreign minister disputed that characterization, calling for an African Union investigation. South Africa is also exploring asking receiving countries to help fund the cost of deportation operations, adding a financial dimension to an already strained regional relationship.

stories.headline: Update: Israel and Iran Exchange Strikes as Ceasefire Collapses on War's 100th Day
stories.summary:
Iran fired ballistic missiles at Israel on Sunday for the first time since a fragile ceasefire took effect on April 8, marking a dramatic collapse of the truce on the 100th day of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. Israel retaliated with airstrikes on military targets in Tehran, Tabriz, and Isfahan early Monday, the first Israeli strikes inside Iran since the ceasefire. Iran had warned that attacks would resume if Israel continued striking Lebanon; the escalation began after Israeli forces bombed suspected Hezbollah strongholds in southern Beirut, killing at least two people.

President Trump, who told NBC's 'Meet the Press' that the two sides were 'very close' to a deal, called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and urged him not to retaliate, saying 'Each of them had their fun.' Netanyahu proceeded with strikes anyway. Two tense calls were exchanged Monday as Trump demanded Israel halt further action; Netanyahu pushed back, according to the Wall Street Journal. Iran also launched ballistic missiles and drones toward Bahrain and Kuwait, with Kuwaiti authorities reporting one person killed and 63 wounded.

Yemen's Houthi rebels separately declared a ban on Israeli ships in the Red Sea, threatening a key bypass route to the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices surged more than 4%, with Brent crude jumping to $97.34 a barrel, while Asian equity markets fell sharply — South Korea's Kospi triggering a circuit breaker after plunging nearly 9% at open. The escalation has put U.S.-Iran negotiations in serious jeopardy and raised the prospect of a return to full-scale regional war.

Supporters of the war effort argue the strikes are a necessary response to Iranian aggression and that Trump's pressure on Netanyahu reflects appropriate diplomatic management of an ally. Critics, including former national security adviser John Bolton, warn that Trump's 'often-contradictory decisions' during the conflict have laid the groundwork for nuclear proliferation in the Middle East. Congressional war powers resolutions in both chambers seek to curb Trump's authority to continue military operations without legislative approval.

stories.headline: Tech Stocks Plunge Globally as AI Selloff, Rate Fears, and Middle East Strikes Converge
stories.summary:
Asian equity markets suffered steep losses Monday as a confluence of pressures — a tech-sector reassessment, fears of U.S. interest rate hikes, and renewed Iran-Israel hostilities — triggered a broad selloff. South Korea's Kospi index plunged nearly 9% at open, activating a circuit-breaker halt for the third time this year, before closing down 8.3%. Japan's Nikkei fell 3.8%, Taiwan's Taiex dropped sharply on weakness in TSMC shares, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng and Shanghai Composite also closed lower.

The selloff follows a roughly 4% drop in the Nasdaq on Friday — its worst single-day decline in more than a year — driven by a stronger-than-expected U.S. jobs report that fueled bets on a Federal Reserve interest rate increase, alongside persistent inflation tied to the Middle East war. Investors have been 'repositioning' over concerns that surging AI-related valuations have outpaced actual revenue generation, according to Saxo chief investment strategist Charu Chanana. Samsung closed down 10% and SK Hynix also fell sharply.

Oil prices accelerated the pressure, with Brent crude rising 4.6% to $97.34 a barrel after Iran and Israel exchanged strikes for the first time since April's ceasefire. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the tech slide presented a buying opportunity, while South Korean President Lee Jae-myung acknowledged expected volatility but called domestic shares 'slightly undervalued.' European markets opened modestly lower, with Germany's Dax off 0.7% and the UK's FTSE 100 down 0.4%.

stories.headline: Starmer Hosts Zelenskyy, Macron, and Merz in London for Ukraine Weapons Summit
stories.summary:
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at 10 Downing Street on Sunday for talks focused on accelerating weapons production to counter Russia's escalating aerial campaign. The meeting came in the wake of a Russian drone strike that killed three people in Ukraine and follows Russia's repeated use of the Oreshnik hypersonic ballistic missile against Ukrainian cities.

In a joint statement, the four leaders condemned Russia's 'large-scale missile and drone attacks' and its 'irresponsible and dangerous' drone incursions into NATO territory, including last month's incident in Romania. They 'underlined the urgent need to scale up the production of interceptors and co-develop anti-ballistic missile and deep strike capabilities,' though no financial details or specific commitments were announced. Zelenskyy stressed that Europe must play a central role in any eventual negotiations to end the war with Russia.

The summit underscores growing European alarm over Russia's weapons advantage at a moment when U.S. attention is heavily focused on the Iran conflict. The meeting produced no concrete funding framework, leaving questions about how the pledged capability-building will be financed and delivered.

stories.headline: Xi Jinping Arrives in Pyongyang for First North Korea Visit in Seven Years
stories.summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Pyongyang on Monday for a rare state visit, his first trip to North Korea in seven years, aimed at reasserting Beijing's influence over an increasingly emboldened ally. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is expected to hold talks with Xi as both nations seek to restore and deepen their traditional alliance at a moment when Pyongyang has developed a closer military partnership with Russia.

The visit comes as North Korea has expanded its nuclear arsenal and deepened ties with Moscow, reportedly supplying ammunition and military personnel in support of Russia's war in Ukraine — a dynamic that has complicated Beijing's regional calculations. Xi's arrival was marked by an elaborate official welcome. The timing, amid the ongoing U.S.-Israel-Iran war and a divided Western security focus, gives both leaders strategic room to reinforce bilateral ties.

The summit carries significant implications for the broader geopolitical landscape, touching on nuclear nonproliferation, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and U.S. Indo-Pacific strategy. Washington and its allies will be watching closely for any formal security commitments or economic agreements that emerge from the talks.
